title: How to Choose a Proof of Concept Development Company (Without Trusting the Rankings)

I didn’t find any. Here’s what governments do instead. Most advice on picking a proof of concept development company goes like this: check the reviews, compare a few quotes, pick someone with experience. It sounds sensible. So I went looking for the evidence behind it. Do companies with higher ratings deliver better proofs of concept? Do bigger agencies? Cheaper ones? Ones in a certain country? I couldn’t find a credible study that says yes to any of those. Not one that states its method, at least. I also couldn’t find a trustworthy failure rate that ties “picked the wrong company” to projects going wrong. That doesn’t mean the choice doesn’t matter. It means most of the usual advice rests on feel, not data. What I did find was something more useful: how US and UK government digital teams, who buy a lot of software and have written down what they learned, decide who to hire. One thing before we start. I work at Entalogics, and we sell this kind of work. Later in this article I’ll recommend starting with a small, paid first phase. That advice happens to help companies like mine, so I’ll lean on public sources instead of my own experience, and I’ll point out where I’m giving you my opinion. What I couldn’t find Let me be clear about the gaps first, because they shape everything else. No data on what predicts success. I found no non-vendor study showing that directory rating, review count, company size, price, location, or whether you hire an agency, a freelancer, an in-house team or a no-code tool, predicts how a proof of concept turns out. No reliable failure rate. You’ll see numbers like “most software projects fail” all over the web. The best-known source, the Standish CHAOS report, was challenged in a 2010 paper in IEEE Software . Its authors, Eveleens and Verhoef, wrote that the report showed “a shocking 16 percent project success. However, Standish’s definitions have four major problems.” I’m not going to quote any of those percentages. No evidence that a paid trial improves outcomes. I’ll recommend one anyway. But it’s expert advice, not something anyone has measured. If a company tells you “X% of founders pick the wrong vendor,” ask where the number comes from. What governments do instead Public digital teams in the US and UK write down how they judge suppliers. Their guidance is built for larger projects than a proof of concept, so you’ll need to scale it down. But the principles carry over. Two caveats on the sources. 18F, the US government team behind much of this guidance, was shut down by the General Services Administration on March 1, 2025, so its guides are archived and won’t be updated. And the UK Government Digital Service’s page on assessing suppliers was published in 2016 and withdrawn on December 31, 2025. I’ll call both historical guidance. They’re still the clearest written statements I found. The shared idea is simple: judge the work, not the pitch. 18F put it this way in its guide to buying software development: “Actual code is a far better indicator of how a vendor team is likely to perform under real-world conditions” than staged exercises like bake-offs or hackathons. The UK guidance suggested you could “ask suppliers to give a practical demonstration of a prototype or discovery kick-off meeting.” The rest of this article is that idea turned into steps. Step 1: Know what you’re buying “Proof of concept” gets used for three different jobs. A proof of concept asks whether a risky piece can be built. A prototype asks whether people will understand and use the idea. A minimum viable product asks whether customers will pay. A good company will ask which one you need before it quotes you. If a company says “yes, we do proofs of concept” and never asks what you’re trying to find out, treat that as a warning. Step 2: Use directories to find names, not to rank them Directories like Clutch and GoodFirms are a fair place to build a shortlist. They’re a poor place to make the final choice, and the platforms are fairly open about why. Clutch’s own methodology page says that paid listings “appear above organic results in directories.” It also describes how reviews get through. If a reviewer’s identity can’t be confirmed but no conflict of interest shows up, the review is “published without a ‘Verified’ badge.” And it says that “in 2025, we rejected 10% of submitted reviews for signs of falsified information.” That’s a useful number in two ways. It shows the platform does check, and it shows people try to cheat. GoodFirms says on its methodology page that sponsorship doesn’t affect its ranking. That’s the platform describing itself, and I couldn’t find an outside audit. What a verified review tells you is that a real client existed and the identity was checked. It doesn’t tell you the work was good. Also, every platform I checked earns money from the companies it lists. Fake reviews are also a legal issue now.
